title: The Rise of the Fusion Democrat
text:
Y ou could use practically any synonym for big to describe this month’s Democratic wins. I’ll go with staggering . For the first time in 145 years, Mississippi will have a Black senator. Roughly three-quarters of the nation’s population will now be led by Democratic governors. In the House, the Democrats expect a roomy 80-plus-seat margin over Republicans. Latinos? Young men? Working-class white people? On Election Day, they all moved left.

 Obviously, the Democrats are delighted. Naturally, they are also fighting. Moderates would like to take credit for this turn in the party’s fortunes, especially in red states. This irks progressives, who point out that many of the winners actually sounded a lot like Bernie Sanders . But a few brave contrarians have also waded into these muddy waters. They argue that there is a different way to look at the results, one that might quell the Democrats’ infighting. Their explanation involves a word that one might expect to see in the context of, say, a corn tortilla stuffed with bulgogi: fusion . Democrats won this year, the progressive pollster Adam Carlson told me, by taking “a little from everyone.”

 The internecine fights over labels might seem petty. Sometimes they are. But for Democrats, these squabbles are crucial. The lessons that the party learns from this election will inform not only how its politicians govern, but also how they behave in the 2028 election cycle, which, if you haven’t heard, is already in full swing.

 M ost Americans showed up to the polls last week fueled by pent-up anger and profound weariness, polling shows. They voted against President Trump and Republican leadership, rather than affirmatively for a bold and beautiful Democratic vision. The political challenge for Democrats now is how to interpret the results: whether the campaigns they ran this cycle should be replicated in 2028—and from which faction of the party the presidential candidates should take their cues. The problem is that these factions are at war, and have been for a long while.

 Progressives say that the mandate belongs to them. They point to the fact that many successful candidates, including Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and James Talarico in Texas, ran on ending corporate corruption and taxing the heck out of America’s billionaires. These winning Democrats, they argue, campaigned using the kind of “fighting oligarchy” message popularized by Sanders and Senator Elizabeth Warren. More data: The Congressional Progressive Caucus will add at least 25 new members, bringing its record-high membership to more than 105; the number of lawmakers who identify as democratic socialists will quadruple, from two to eight. “If those who call themselves moderate want to slap their label on candidates who campaigned on our issues, then cool—we’ve won the battle for the heart, soul, and future direction of the party,” Adam Green, a co-founder of the Progressive Change Institute, said when the group released its postelection analysis.

 Moderates, unfortunately for Green, do want to slap their label on those candidates. They point out that economic populism is a long-standing principle of the Democratic Party, not a concept owned by progressives. They also note that the Democrats who flipped Republican Senate seats found ways to signal their independence from progressive orthodoxy. In Texas, for example, Talarico embraced the oil industry. In Iowa, Josh Turek campaigned on border security, and opposed allowing transgender women to play in women’s sports. None of the successful red-state Senate Democrats endorsed Medicare for All. “The lesson from this cycle is unequivocal: high-quality Democrats in the middle were the majority makers in 2026—and they are the model for 2028,” reads one analysis from the centrist think tank Third Way. The Blue Dog Coalition, a tiny House caucus of moderate Democrats, will more than double next year, expanding to at least 22 members.

 [ Read: The GOP’s culture-war Hail Mary ] 

 But a third group of Democrats is attempting to make peace between the factions. These Democrats believe that their candidates won because they managed to combine some of the best ideas from both camps—baking a moderate cake and slathering it with a fluffy layer of progressivism. What if—and hear them out—Democrats can have it all? “This election points toward a new liberal fusionism, candidates who combine leftist economic populism with centrist pragmatism,” Rotimi Adeoye, a member of the New York Times editorial board, wrote on X on November 4. He pronounced factional fighting, a feature of today’s Democratic Party, to be “old news, beltway chatter.” Some of the freshman lawmakers are already showing what fusion might look like in practical terms. Sam Forstag, a former smokejumper from Montana, for example, plans to join both the Blue Dogs and the Congressional Progressive Caucus.

 Fusionism was a Republican thing first. Former President Ronald Reagan was big on the concept, which was developed by the political philosopher Frank Meyer and promoted by the National Review editor William F. Buckley Jr. For Republicans, fusion meant blending traditional social conservatism with free-market libertarianism. For Democrats, it looks more like pairing socially moderate positions (don’t let transgender girls play girls’ sports; protect the border) with progressive economic ones (raise the minimum wage; tax the rich).

 Proponents of fusionism love Senator Jon Ossoff of Georgia, who talked nonstop about political and corporate corruption during his campaign for reelection, while simultaneously opposing several progressive priorities, such as Medicare for All, abolishing ICE , and expanding the Supreme Court. Talarico, too: The Texas state lawmaker repeated the line that the “only minority destroying America is the billionaires” but also criticized former President Biden for failing to secure the border, and moderated his position on the inclusion of trans kids in sports.

 [ Read: Jon Ossoff is doing something different ] 

 Carlson, the pollster, believes that the combine-and-stir formulation can work well for Democrats. He’s listed a few priorities from the winning 2026 campaigns that he hopes become part of the blueprint for the national party: rooting out corruption, naming billionaires as the enemy, showing empathy on transgender issues, reclaiming patriotism, securing the border, and regulating AI companies. (Representative Sarah McBride of Delaware also appears to be a Fusion Head: “Co-sign. Spot on,” she responded to Carlson.)

 Other Democrats prefer to use different language. Adam Jentleson refers to this kind of mix-and-match thinking as “heterodox.” His think tank, Searchlight Institute, argues that to win a supermajority again in Congress, Democrats should not rigidly adhere to a set of positions simply because they’re on the party platform. After all, the opinions of the average American voter do not line up neatly along ideological lines. “Fusion, heterodoxy, call it whatever you want, but we are leaving the past behind and forging a new model,” Jentleson told me.

 T he problem with labels is that they are annoying and academic. Do we really need more of them? The progressive strategist Rebecca Katz groaned when I asked for her thoughts on “fusionism” and “heterodoxy.” Her candidates rejected such ideological labels, she told me. She described one of them, Gina Hinojosa, the Texas Democrat who just defeated Governor Greg Abbott, as “post-partisan.” (This certainly sounds like another label, but I’ll let it slide.) Hinojosa campaigned almost exclusively on economic issues, Katz said, but she managed to win without moderating on social ones. “Did she throw trans kids under the bus? I don’t think so.”

 Moderate Democrats argue that “fusionism” as a concept is redundant—that embracing a mix of progressive and pragmatic positions is what they already do . And they see this month’s wins as evidence that the party should continue to practice that moderation ahead of 2028.

 Ideological categories aside, the Democrats seem to have identified a winning combination of positions—or, at least, a combination that won this time. The task ahead has less to do with labels, and much more to do with showing voters how Democrats will actually use their political power. Will they govern like progressives, or like moderates? Perhaps they’ll try to do a little bit of both.
